name: Aaron Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Glad to. I'm Aaron, I'm 27, and I'm the shepherd on Mrs Hale's hill farm. It's a mixed farm, but mostly sheep: about 900 ewes up on the hill, a few suckler cows lower down, and the hay meadows by the river.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I check the weather model on my phone, then go up the hill on the quad with my two dogs, Moss and Fly. Every ewe has an electronic ear tag, so when we bring them through the race, the reader logs her weight and lambing record straight onto the laptop. I've started flying a drone to find stragglers in the bracken, which saves the dogs a lot of running. Lambing in April is three weeks of hardly sleeping, and I love it and hate it in equal measure. What I really love is being on the top of the hill at six with nobody else for ten miles.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. It helps me read the weather, sort the flock records and fill in the subsidy forms, which used to take me a whole wet Sunday. I live on my own in the shepherd's cottage, which comes with the job. I've got about three weeks of wages saved and there's hardly any other farm work in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, I'd keep using what I use. It's already useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good and anyone who isn't using them is making life harder for themselves. I'd still say that at the auction mart, even if the big promises came to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved for the valley. There are older men here who'd be lost if things changed fast, and I'd rather they kept their dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the drone and the records and maybe save up for a second drone with a speaker on it, so I can call the dogs from the air. I'd start putting away a bit each month towards a flock of my own, maybe 100 ewes on rented land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a flock of your own. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the dream. My grandad had his own flock and lost it in a bad year. I'd like to get the family name back on a few sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the dogs still have a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would. The dogs know the hill better than any machine. The drone just finds the sheep, the dogs still move them.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are good and anyone not using them is making life harder for themselves. I'd still say it at the auction mart, even if the big promises came to nothing.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved for the valley. Some of the older men here would be lost if things changed fast, and I'd rather they kept their dignity.
S0.do: Keeps using the drone and digital flock records and saves for a second drone. Starts putting a little away each month towards a flock of about 100 ewes of his own on rented land.
S0.quote: My grandad had his own flock and lost it in a bad year. I'd like to get the family name back on a few sheep.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is an everyday AI user in a very traditional setting, and he sees no conflict between the two. His long-term goal is to rebuild the family flock his grandfather lost. He worries about the older men in the valley more than about himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That feels about right. And I'd be ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for hill farms, because we've always had too few hands. I'd tell the young farmers' club to learn the tools now, and I'd show anyone who asks how I use mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. The hill is the last place a robot will manage, because of the bogs and the bracken and the weather. So for a while I'd be the man who knows both the hill and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Hale to put money into virtual fencing collars for the ewes, so they stay off the neighbour's ground without walls being rebuilt. I'd offer drone gathering to the next three farms at a day rate. And I'd keep saving for my own sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit cocky, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You believe in free markets, but hill farming relies on public payments. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. We live on subsidies, and I'm not keen on handouts. I'd say the payments should be for looking after the land, which is work, not for doing nothing. But yes, it's a sore point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the valley would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Bill, who's shepherded the next farm for forty years. He'd see my drone and think I was showing off. I'd want to help him, but he wouldn't ask.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for hill farms, because we've always had too few hands. I'd tell the young farmers' club to learn the tools now and show anyone how I use mine.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because the hill is the last place a robot will manage with its bogs, bracken and weather. For a while I'd be the man who knows both the hill and the machines.
S1.do: Asks his employer to invest in virtual fencing collars for the ewes and offers drone gathering to three neighbouring farms at a day rate. Keeps saving for his own flock.
S1.quote: The hill is the last place a robot will manage, because of the bogs and the bracken and the weather.
S1.fieldNote: He expects to gain from gradual change and admits to some swagger. When I raised the gap between his free-market views and hill farm subsidies, he called the payments a reward for land care, not handouts, and accepted it was a sore point. He worries about an older neighbour too proud to ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then nothing's safe, not even the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families and villages have to pull together, like they did in the bad winters. I'd say we look after our own and we don't wait for the government to save us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the hill becomes one more job a robot can do. A drone that gathers, a collar that fences and an AI that reads the flock means Mrs Hale doesn't need a shepherd, just someone to change batteries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself that someone. I'd buy into whatever gear I could afford, get every certificate going for drones and robots, and offer the service to every hill farm in the valley before a big company does. I'd probably also take the cottage question to Mrs Hale straight away, because if the job goes, so does my roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fighting. Like a ewe stuck in a snowdrift, kicking because she won't give up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the money runs out before the service takes off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my mum and sister, and on the chapel. We'd share what we have. I'd sooner do that than queue for help, though I'm not too proud to take it if there's nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the plan for your own flock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel that. My grandad's flock, gone in one bad year. Mine would be gone before it started.

S2.say: I'd say families and villages have to pull together, like in the bad winters. We look after our own and don't wait for the government to save us.
S2.think: I think the hill becomes one more job a robot can do. A drone, a collar and an AI reading the flock means Mrs Hale needs someone to change batteries, not a shepherd.
S2.do: Buys what kit he can afford, gets every drone and robot certificate going and offers the service to every hill farm before a big company does. Raises the tied cottage with his employer at once and leans on family and chapel if money runs out.
S2.feel: Anxious but fighting, like a ewe kicking in a snowdrift.
S2.quote: Mrs Hale doesn't need a shepherd, just someone to change batteries.
S2.fieldNote: Even with two years, his instinct is to move fast and become the operator rather than the person replaced. His tied cottage is a hidden risk he names quickly. The lost family flock comes back as a personal grief, and his safety net is family and chapel before the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a race, but a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young people in the hills should learn these machines now, and that families should help each other buy in rather than sell to outsiders. That's how we kept the farms going last time things got hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build a small business and maybe even my own flock run with robots. I'd be the shepherd who owns the machines instead of the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd get my drone licence upgraded and start the gathering service on a few farms. By year two I'd want a small loan to buy collars and a second drone, and I'd rent some hill ground for my first 100 ewes. By year four I'd hope to employ a lad from the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit anxious. More excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a big company does the same thing cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. But I'd still have the ground, the sheep and the business. And I'd rather sell to my neighbours than have some company from the city do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd employ someone. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd want. A lad who'd learn the hill and the machines both, so there's still a young person in the valley.

S3.say: I'd say young people in the hills should learn these machines now, and families should help each other buy in rather than sell to outsiders. That's how we kept farms going before.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build a small business and maybe my own flock run with robots. I'd be the shepherd who owns the machines instead of the one they replace.
S3.do: Upgrades his drone licence and starts a gathering service in year one, then takes a small loan for collars and a second drone in year two while renting ground for 100 ewes. Hopes to employ a young person from the village by year four.
S3.feel: Excited and a bit anxious, more excited.
S3.quote: I'd be the shepherd who owns the machines instead of the one they replace.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a business plan and a path back to his own flock. He wants to employ someone local, partly to keep young people in the valley. He prefers neighbours and family to outsiders, which fits his traditional outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've no excuse. Ten years is long enough to train every young farmer in the valley and keep the land in local hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the picture where I win. I'd have my own flock, my own machines and maybe a family by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build it slowly: the drone service first, my own 100 ewes by year three, and buy collars only once the prices come down. I'd save properly, at least a hundred a month, so I'm never one bad winter away from losing it all like my grandad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a family. Is that part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd want to marry and have children by then, and I'd want them to grow up on the hill, with dogs, even if the drone does the gathering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The valley itself. If every farm needs only one person, the school closes, the chapel empties and the pub shuts. I'd want my kids to have somewhere to grow up.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years. That's long enough to train every young farmer in the valley and keep the land in local hands.
S4.think: Ten years is the picture where I win. I'd have my own flock, my own machines and maybe a family by then.
S4.do: Builds the drone service first and his own 100 ewes by year three, buying collars only once prices fall. Saves at least a hundred a month and plans to marry and start a family.
S4.quote: If every farm needs only one person, the school closes, the chapel empties and the pub shuts.
S4.fieldNote: In the long picture his personal worries fade and he sees himself winning. His remaining worry is the community: fewer workers per farm could hollow out the valley. He links his saving plans directly to his grandfather losing the family flock.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd lose the job and the cottage before I could build anything. What would help is small, cheap loans for young farmers to buy their own machines, and keeping the land in local hands so the valley stays alive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. Moss and Fly do a job no machine has matched yet. I'm not sure what happens to them, or to people like me, if nobody needs a dog on the hill any more.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thanks. The dogs will be wondering where I've got to.

headlineQuote: I'd be the shepherd who owns the machines instead of the one they replace.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old shepherd who runs about 900 ewes on a hill farm, living alone in a cottage that comes with the job and holding about three weeks of savings. He uses AI and drones every day, yet his values are traditional: family, chapel, self-reliance and keeping land in local hands. In most pictures he plans to move first and own the machines, starting with a drone gathering service and working towards rebuilding the flock his grandfather lost. The two-year picture makes him anxious because the job and his home would go together. Even when he wins, he worries that the valley's school, chapel and pub would empty.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because he would lose both his job and his cottage before he could build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Small, cheap loans for young farmers to buy their own machines, and keeping land in local hands so the valley stays alive.
